Content:
Suppose we want to find the intersection of the surface [MATH: z = f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2] with the plane [MATH: z=4.]

Content:
To find the intersection, we set both equations equal to each other:
[MATH: x^2 + y^2 = 4]

Content:
Graphing the above equation in the [MATH: xy]-plane, we get a circle [MATH: \color{black} C] with center at [MATH: (0,0)] and radius [MATH: 2.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b7779f570348c0afd6b978fe47c0457f]

Content:
The curve [MATH: \color{black} C] is called a level curve of the surface [MATH: z = x^2 + y^2.] The level curves of the form
[MATH: x^2 + y^2 = c]
for [MATH: c=1,2,3,4] are shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d3eacd45014cc871dc5fab766eb1c60e]

Content:
The diagram above is called a contour plot. The level curves are sometimes called contours.

Content:
In general, a level curve [MATH: L_{c}(f)] of a real-valued function of two variables [MATH: f(x,y)] is any set of the form

Content:
[MATH: L_{c}(f) = \left\{(x,y) \, : \,f(x,y)=c\right\}]
where [MATH: c] is a constant.

Content:
Note: In our example, [MATH: x^2 +y^2 \ge 0] for all [MATH: (x,y),] which means that the sets [MATH: L_{c}(f)] are nonempty for [MATH: c \ge 0.]

items.title: Finding the Equation of a Level Curve

sections.normalized_html: Find the equation of the level curve that passes through the point [MATH: G\big(\sqrt{5}, 1\big)] for the function [MATH: f(x,y) = \dfrac{12y}{x^2-y^2}.]
sections.readable_text: Find the equation of the level curve that passes through the point [MATH: G\big(\sqrt{5}, 1\big)] for the function [MATH: f(x,y) = \dfrac{12y}{x^2-y^2}.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find the value of the function at [MATH: G]: [MATH: \eqalign{ f\big(\sqrt{5}, 1\big)&= \dfrac{12(1)}{\big(\sqrt{5}\big)^2 - 1^2} = 3}]

Hence, the level curve that passes through [MATH: G\big(\sqrt{5}, 1\big)] is the [MATH: 3]-level curve.

Recall that the level curves for the function [MATH: f(x,y)] are given by the equation [MATH: f(x,y) = c.]

In our case, we're interested in [MATH: c=3.] So, we have:

[MATH: f(x, y)|= c; (12y)/(x^{2} − y^{2})|= 3; 4y|= x^{2} − y^{2}; x^{2} − y^{2} − 4y − 4|= − 4; x^{2} − (y^{2} + 4y + 4)|= − 4; x^{2} − (y + 2)^{2}|= − 4]

Therefore, the level curve that passes through [MATH: G\big(\sqrt{5}, 1\big)] is the hyperbola [MATH: x^2 - (y+2)^2 = -4.]

sections.normalized_html:
The level curves of the function [MATH: f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2+2y^2-2}{x^2}] are given by [MATH: f(x,y) = c.] Which of the following statements are true?

  1. [MATH: c=1] gives a circle

  2. [MATH: c=0] gives an ellipse

  3. [MATH: c=2] gives a hyperbola
sections.readable_text:
The level curves of the function [MATH: f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2+2y^2-2}{x^2}] are given by [MATH: f(x,y) = c.] Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: c=1] gives a circle
2. [MATH: c=0] gives an ellipse
3. [MATH: c=2] gives a hyperbola

sections.normalized_html:
Setting [MATH: f(x,y) = c] gives

[MATH: (x^{2} + 2y^{2} − 2)/(x^{2})|= c; x^{2} + 2y^{2} − 2|= cx^{2}; (1 − c)x^{2} + 2y^{2}|= 2.]

Therefore:

  • If [MATH: c = 1,] then the level curve is [MATH: y^2 = 1,] which consists of two lines.

  • If [MATH: c = 0,] then the level curve is [MATH: x^2+2y^2=2,] which is an ellipse.

  • If [MATH: c = 2,] then the level curve is [MATH: 2y^2-x^2=2] which is a hyperbola.

So, only statements II and III are true.

Note that we must have the constraint [MATH: c\gt 0] since [MATH: e^x \gt 0] for all [MATH: x.]

Therefore, we have

[MATH: e^{x^{2} − y^{2}} = c; \ln (e^{x^{2} − y^{2}}) = \ln c; x^{2} − y^{2} = \ln c.]

We can split this into three cases, depending on the sign of [MATH: \ln c.]

  • Case 1: [MATH: \ln c \gt 0.] In this case, we have the family of hyperbolas [MATH: x^2-y^2 = \ln c.]

  • Case 2: [MATH: \ln c = 0.] In this case, we have the lines [MATH: y=\pm x.]

  • Case 3: [MATH: \ln c < 0.] In this case, we have the family of hyperbolas [MATH: y^2 - x^2 = -\ln c.]

Therefore, the level curves are as follows:
